Admit it to prove ownership or control, with a limiting instruction against using it to infer negligence.
Exclude it, because insurance is admissible only to show a witness's bias.
oe: Rule 411 bars only one purpose: proving negligence or wrongful conduct.
That is the barred purpose.
Rule 411 has no such prerequisite. Ownership and control are independent permitted purposes.

Correct. Rule 411 permits insurance evidence for "another purpose," including "agency, ownership, or control." Lund disputes control, and insuring the dock tends to show it. A Rule 105 instruction limits the jury's use.
Bias is one example. Rule 411 also lists agency, ownership, and control.
questions.e: Rule 411 bars insurance evidence only to prove negligence or wrongful conduct. It may be admitted for another purpose, such as bias, agency, ownership, or control, subject to Rule 403 and a limiting instruction.

questions.tag: Biaggi: rejecting immunity as consciousness of innocence
questions.q:
Paul Mariner, a company CEO, is on trial for bribery. Before indictment, prosecutors offered him immunity in exchange for information about other executives' payments. He replied that he knew of no payments by anyone, and the offer was withdrawn. At trial, the government proved consciousness of guilt by showing that Mariner moved large sums into gold after colleagues began cooperating. Mariner offers evidence of his rejection of immunity. The government objects that it is irrelevant and is plea-negotiation material.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude it, because Rule 410 bars any evidence of plea or immunity discussions.
Exclude it, because declining an offer has no tendency to show innocence.
Admit it only if Mariner testifies and is subject to cross-examination.
Exclude it, because it is self-serving hearsay.
Admit it, because rejecting an offer of immunity tends to show consciousness of innocence, and Rule 410 protects defendants, not the government.
oe: Rule 410 bars use "against the defendant." It doesn't stop the defendant from offering his own conduct.
Biaggi distinguished rejecting a plea to a lesser charge, which may be a gamble, from rejecting immunity, which strongly suggests a lack of guilty knowledge.
The evidence can be proved through others. Biaggi imposed no such condition.
His rejection is offered as conduct showing consciousness of innocence, not to prove the truth of an assertion.

Correct. United States v. Biaggi reversed the exclusion of this evidence. Rejecting immunity is probative of innocence, and fairness required admitting it once the government proved consciousness of guilt. Rule 410 protects the defendant who negotiated.
questions.e: Rule 410 shields the defendant, not the government. Under Biaggi, a defendant's rejection of immunity is relevant to consciousness of innocence, especially when the government offers consciousness-of-guilt evidence.

questions.tag: Rule 404(a)(2)(A): the trait must be pertinent
questions.q:
Oscar Keene is charged with federal income-tax evasion. In his defense, he offers: (1) a neighbor's testimony that Keene has a reputation as a peaceful, gentle man; and (2) a business associate's opinion that Keene is honest and law-abiding. The government objects to both.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit both, because a criminal defendant may offer evidence of any good character trait.
Exclude both, because character evidence is inadmissible to prove conduct on a particular occasion.
Admit (2) only, because honesty and law-abidingness are pertinent to tax evasion and peacefulness isn't.
Admit (1) only, because reputation is a more reliable form of proof than opinion.
Exclude both unless Keene first testifies.
oe: Rule 404(a)(2)(A) admits only a "pertinent" trait, one relevant to the crime charged.
Rule 404(a)(2)(A) is an exception: the accused may offer a pertinent trait to show action in conformity.

Correct. Under Rule 404(a)(2)(A), the accused may offer a pertinent trait. Honesty and law-abidingness bear on tax evasion, which is a crime of deceit. Peacefulness doesn't, so it is irrelevant. Both items use proper forms under Rule 405(a).
Rule 405(a) allows reputation or opinion equally. And peacefulness isn't pertinent to tax evasion.
The accused may offer character witnesses without testifying.
questions.e: Under Rule 404(a)(2)(A), an accused may offer evidence of a pertinent trait, one relevant to the charged crime, in reputation or opinion form (Rule 405(a)). Doing so lets the prosecution rebut it.

questions.tag: Self-defense: the victim's violence the defendant knew of
questions.q:
Nadia Fox is charged with murdering Ray Doyle, and she claims self-defense. She offers:

I. Her own testimony that two weeks before the killing, Doyle told her he had stabbed a man outside a bar.
II. Testimony from Doyle's former coworker, whom Fox never met, that Doyle once broke the coworker's jaw.
III. A witness's opinion that Doyle was a violent person.

Which items are admissible?
o: I only.
II only.
I and III only.
II and III only.
I, II, and III.
oe: Item III is also admissible. Rule 404(a)(2)(B) lets an accused offer the victim's pertinent trait in opinion form.
Item II is a specific act Fox didn't know about. It can only show Doyle's character, and specific instances aren't a permitted form here.

Correct. Item I goes to Fox's state of mind: what she heard bears on whether her fear was reasonable, which is a non-character, non-hearsay use (compare United States v. James). Item III is the victim's pertinent trait in opinion form under Rules 404(a)(2)(B) and 405(a). Item II is a specific act offered only to prove character. Character isn't an essential element of self-defense, so Rule 405(b) doesn't admit it.
Item I is admissible to show Fox's reasonable fear. Item II isn't, because Rule 405(a) limits proof of the victim's character to reputation or opinion.
Item II fails. Specific instances prove character only on cross or when character is an essential element (Rule 405(b)).
questions.e: Violent acts of the victim that the defendant knew of are admissible to show the defendant's reasonable fear. To prove the victim's violent character, the accused may offer reputation or opinion (Rules 404(a)(2)(B), 405(a)). Character isn't an element of self-defense, so Rule 405(b) doesn't apply.

questions.tag: Weil: deliberate conduct isn't habit
questions.q:
Ada Price sues her allergist, Dr. Seltz, alleging that for years he gave her steroid pills while telling her they were antihistamines. To prove he deceived her, she offers testimony from six other long-term patients that Dr. Seltz told each of them the same thing about the same pills. Dr. Seltz has treated thousands of patients.

What is the most accurate statement about the evidence?
o: It is admissible under Rule 406 as habit, because the doctor repeated the same statement to several patients.
It isn't habit, because deliberate, morally charged conduct shown with a few patients is neither regular nor semi-automatic. It is admissible only for a non-propensity purpose under Rule 404(b).
It is inadmissible, because Rule 404 bars all evidence of other acts in civil cases.
It is admissible to show the doctor's propensity to deceive, because the propensity ban applies only in criminal cases.
It is admissible as routine practice of the doctor's medical practice under Rule 406.
oe: Repetition alone doesn't make habit. Habit is a regular, semi-automatic response to a recurring situation.

Correct. Weil held that a doctor's deceptions of eight patients weren't habit: they were deliberate, they varied by patient, and eight out of a large practice isn't "regular." Such evidence may come in, if at all, under Rule 404(b)(2) for a purpose such as intent or plan, subject to Rule 403.
Rule 404 applies in civil cases, but Rule 404(b)(2) permits other acts for non-propensity purposes.
The character ban in Rule 404 applies in civil cases too.
An organization's routine practice must be regular and systematic. A few instances out of thousands of patients don't qualify.
questions.e: Under Rule 406, habit is a specific, regular, semi-automatic response to a recurring situation. Deliberate, morally charged conduct is usually character (Weil), admissible only through a Rule 404(b)(2) purpose.

questions.tag: Rule 404(b)(3): notice in a criminal case
questions.q:
Midway through a federal wire-fraud trial in which Lena Hart claims she didn't know the investment was a sham, the prosecutor seeks to prove that Hart ran a similar scheme in 2021, to show intent and knowledge. The prosecutor gave no pretrial notice. She explains that she had the 2021 file for months but "didn't think we'd need it." The defense never asked for notice.

What is the proper ruling?
o: Admit it, because the prosecution must give notice of other-acts evidence only if the defense requests it.
Admit it, because intent is always at issue in a fraud prosecution, so notice is unnecessary.
Exclude it, because the notice requirement applies to all other-acts evidence in civil and criminal cases.
Admit it, because the notice rule applies only to evidence offered under Rules 413–415.
Exclude it, because the prosecution gave no reasonable written notice before trial and has shown no good cause for the delay.
oe: That was the rule before 2020. Rule 404(b)(3) now requires notice in every criminal case, with no request needed.
Intent may be a proper purpose, but that doesn't excuse the notice requirement.
Rule 404(b)(3) applies only "in a criminal case."
Rules 413–415 have their own 15-day disclosure rule. Rule 404(b)(3) separately governs ordinary other-acts evidence.

Correct. Rule 404(b)(3) requires the prosecutor to give reasonable written notice before trial, stating the permitted purpose and the reasoning behind it. Notice during trial is allowed only if the court excuses pretrial notice for good cause, and having the file all along isn't good cause.
questions.e: Rule 404(b)(3) requires the prosecutor in a criminal case to give reasonable written notice of other-acts evidence before trial, stating the permitted purpose and the reasoning, unless the court excuses it for good cause. No defense request is needed.

questions.tag: Rule 609(e): a conviction on appeal
questions.q:
Cole Dunbar is on trial for assault and testifies in his own defense. Fourteen months ago he was convicted of federal mail fraud, which requires proof of a scheme to defraud by false representations, and his appeal of that conviction is pending. The prosecution offers the conviction to impeach. Dunbar asks that it be excluded until the appeal is decided, or else that he be allowed to tell the jury about the appeal.

What is the correct ruling?
o: Exclude the conviction until the appeal is resolved, because it isn't yet final.
Admit the conviction only if its probative value outweighs its prejudicial effect to Dunbar.
Admit the conviction, and bar any mention of the appeal as confusing.
Exclude the conviction, because fraud isn't similar to assault.
Admit the conviction, and allow Dunbar to show that the appeal is pending.
oe: Rule 609(e) says a conviction is admissible "even if an appeal is pending."
Mail fraud's elements require proof of a false statement, so Rule 609(a)(2) mandates admission without balancing.
Rule 609(e) expressly says that "evidence of the pendency is also admissible."
Rule 609(a)(2) admits crimen falsi regardless of how similar it is to the charge. And here the lack of similarity would only favor admission.

Correct. Mail fraud is crimen falsi, so Rule 609(a)(2) requires admission with no balancing. Under Rule 609(e), a pending appeal doesn't bar use of the conviction, and the pendency is also admissible.
questions.e: Under Rule 609(a)(2), a conviction whose elements required a dishonest act or false statement must be admitted. Under Rule 609(e), a pending appeal doesn't bar it, and the pendency is admissible too.

questions.tag: Rule 613(a): showing the statement
questions.q:
In a shooting trial, prosecution eyewitness Tess Ames testifies that she clearly saw the defendant's face. On cross, defense counsel asks: "Didn't you text your cousin the next morning, 'I never saw the shooter's face'?" The prosecutor objects that counsel must first show Ames the text. Defense counsel refuses, and the prosecutor then asks to see the text.

How should the court rule?
o: Sustain the objection, because a witness must be shown a prior written statement before being asked about it.
Overrule the objection, because the text isn't hearsay, and defense counsel never has to show it to anyone.
Sustain the objection, because Rule 613(b) requires a foundation before any inquiry.
Overrule the objection, and order defense counsel to show the text to the prosecutor on request.
Overrule the objection, but forbid any later extrinsic proof of the text.
oe: That was the common-law rule of the Queen's Case. Rule 613(a) abolishes it.
The non-hearsay point is right, but Rule 613(a) requires disclosure to opposing counsel on request.
Rule 613(b) governs extrinsic evidence of a prior inconsistent statement, not questioning the witness about it.

Correct. Under Rule 613(a), a party examining a witness about a prior statement need not show it or disclose its contents to the witness. But it must, on request, show or disclose it to an adverse party's attorney.
If Ames denies sending the text, extrinsic proof is allowed on this non-collateral point, after she has had a chance to explain or deny it (Rule 613(b), as amended in 2024).
questions.e: Under Rule 613(a), the examiner needn't show a prior statement to the witness but must disclose it to opposing counsel on request. Under Rule 613(b), extrinsic proof requires an opportunity to explain or deny, ordinarily given first since 2024.

questions.tag: Contradiction on a collateral matter
questions.q:
In a convenience-store robbery trial, eyewitness Omar Haddad testifies that he saw the robbery as he was walking past the store, and adds that he was wearing his red raincoat that night. The defense calls Haddad's roommate, who would testify that Haddad's only raincoat is blue and that he wore it that night. Nothing else turns on the coat's color.

What is the proper ruling on the roommate's testimony?
o: Admit it, because a witness may always be contradicted by extrinsic evidence.
Exclude it, because extrinsic evidence offered only to contradict a witness on a collateral matter is generally barred.
Admit it under Rule 608(b), because it shows that Haddad lies.
Exclude it, because contradiction isn't a permitted method of impeachment.
Admit it, because matters affecting a witness's credibility are never collateral.
oe: Contradiction on a collateral point may be explored on cross, but extrinsic proof usually isn't allowed.

Correct. The coat's color is relevant only to contradict Haddad. Under the collateral-matter principle, extrinsic proof on such a point is generally excluded, and Rule 403 supports that. The defense may cross-examine about it but must take his answer.
Rule 608(b) bars extrinsic evidence of specific acts offered to attack character for truthfulness, so it points against admission, not toward it.
Contradiction is one of the "lying now" modes of impeachment. It is limited, not forbidden.
Only bias is never collateral (Abel). A mistaken detail is.
questions.e: Under the collateral-matter principle, extrinsic evidence offered only to contradict a witness on a point with no independent relevance is generally barred. Bias and non-collateral contradictions may be proved extrinsically.

questions.tag: A prior false accusation isn't sexual behavior
questions.q:
Grant Ellis is charged with sexual assault. He wants to cross-examine the complainant about an accusation of rape she made against another man three years ago, which she recanted in a signed statement to police. The prosecution moves to exclude it under Rule 412.

What is the correct analysis?
o: Rule 412 bars it, because the accusation concerns the complainant's other sexual behavior.
It is admissible only if excluding it would violate Ellis's constitutional rights.
Rule 412 doesn't apply. The court asks whether a jury could reasonably find the accusation false, then applies Rule 403 and Rule 608(b)'s limits.
It is admissible only if Ellis proves the earlier accusation false by clear and convincing evidence.
It is admissible, and Ellis may prove the accusation through the other man's testimony even if the complainant admits it.
oe: A false accusation is speech, not sexual behavior or predisposition, so Rule 412 doesn't reach it.
Rule 412(b)(1)(C) is needed only for evidence Rule 412 would otherwise bar.

Correct. A prior false accusation isn't "sexual behavior," so Rule 412 doesn't apply. The threshold is whether a jury could find the accusation false (State v. Smith, La. 1999, using the Huddleston standard). It may then be explored on cross under Rule 608(b), subject to Rule 403.
Courts borrow Huddleston's sufficiency standard: could a jury reasonably find it false?
Offered to show untruthfulness, the act is a Rule 608(b) specific instance. Extrinsic proof is barred, and the examiner takes the answer.
questions.e: Rule 412 doesn't reach a prior false accusation, which isn't sexual behavior. Its admission turns on whether a jury could find it false, then Rule 608(b) (cross only, no extrinsic proof) and Rule 403.

questions.tag: A witness's own earlier words
questions.q:
In her suit over an intersection collision, Hannah Lowe testifies that the defendant ran a red light. She then adds: "The next morning I told my sister, 'That other driver ran a red light.'" Lowe offers the sister conversation to prove the light was red. The defense hasn't suggested that Lowe fabricated her account or that her memory is faulty.

Is the testimony about what she told her sister admissible?
o: Yes, because Lowe is testifying and can be cross-examined about her own statement.
Yes, as a present sense impression.
Yes, as an opposing party's statement, because Lowe is a party.
Yes, as a prior consistent statement.
No, because it is hearsay and no exception or exclusion applies.
oe: Hearsay is a statement the declarant doesn't make "while testifying at the current trial." A witness repeating her own earlier words is still offering hearsay.
Rule 803(1) requires a statement made while or immediately after perceiving the event. The next morning is too late.
Rule 801(d)(2) applies only to statements offered against the party who made them. Lowe is offering her own statement.
Rule 801(d)(1)(B) admits a consistent statement only to rebut a charge of fabrication or improper motive, or to rehabilitate after an attack on another ground. Neither has occurred.

Correct. Lowe's out-of-court statement, offered to prove the light was red, is hearsay even though she now testifies. It fits no exception: it's too late for Rule 803(1), not offered against her, and not offered to rebut an attack under Rule 801(d)(1)(B).
questions.e: A testifying witness's own prior statement offered for its truth is hearsay unless it fits Rule 801(d)(1) or an exception. Prior consistent statements need an attack on credibility, and party statements must be offered against the party.

questions.tag: Absence of complaints: nonassertive silence
questions.q:
In a products suit claiming that the Zephyr blender's lid flies off during use, the manufacturer calls its customer-service director. She personally handles every complaint the company receives. She testifies that in three years of sales, about 40,000 Zephyr blenders sold under similar conditions, no customer has reported a lid coming off. The plaintiff objects that the testimony is hearsay.

How should the court rule?
o: Overrule the objection, because the customers' silence isn't conduct they intended as an assertion, so it isn't hearsay.
Sustain the objection, because the silence implies that the customers believed the lids were safe.
Sustain the objection unless the company offers its complaint records under Rule 803(7).
Overrule the objection, because evidence of a manufacturer's good safety record is character evidence admissible in civil cases.
Sustain the objection, because absence of complaints can never be relevant to safety.
oe: Correct. Under Rule 801(a), nonverbal conduct is a statement only if intended as an assertion. Customers who simply didn't complain intended to assert nothing, like the paramedics' silence in the course examples. The testimony isn't hearsay, and the director has personal knowledge. Relevance depends on similar conditions, subject to Rule 403.
The Federal Rules rejected the implied-assertion approach of Wright. Unintended inferences from conduct aren't statements.
Rule 803(7) is one route for proving absence through records, but the director testifies from personal knowledge, and the silence isn't hearsay in the first place.
This isn't character evidence about a person. Its admissibility turns on hearsay and relevance.
With a foundation showing similar conditions and a reliable reporting channel, the absence of complaints has a tendency to show safety.
questions.e: Under Rule 801(a), only conduct intended as an assertion is a statement. Silence or nonassertive conduct isn't hearsay, though it must still be relevant and pass Rule 403.

questions.tag: Pre-arrest silence to impeach
questions.q:
Kurt Rowe shot Leon Ivers on May 3. Rowe didn't contact police, and he was arrested on May 17 and given Miranda warnings, after which he stayed silent. At trial Rowe testifies for the first time that Ivers attacked him with a knife. On cross, the prosecutor asks: (1) "In the two weeks before your arrest, you never went to police to report that you'd been attacked, did you?" and (2) "And after your arrest and warnings, you never told the detectives about any knife, did you?"

Which questions are proper?
o: Both, because a defendant who testifies waives any objection to questions about his silence.
Neither, because using a defendant's silence against him always violates the Fifth Amendment.
(2) only, because silence after Miranda warnings is the most probative.
(1) only, because only post-Miranda silence is protected from impeachment use.
Neither, because silence can't be an adoptive admission unless the defendant was accused to his face.
oe: Testifying doesn't open post-Miranda silence to impeachment (Doyle).
Pre-arrest silence may be used to impeach a testifying defendant (Jenkins). The constitutional bar of Doyle covers silence after Miranda warnings.
Doyle forbids exactly that question. Post-Miranda silence is "insolubly ambiguous," and the warnings implicitly promise it won't be penalized.

Correct. Doyle bars impeachment with silence after Miranda warnings. Pre-arrest silence carries no such implied promise and may be used to impeach a testifying defendant whose story, if true, one would have expected him to report.
Question (1) isn't offered as an adoptive admission but to impeach Rowe's trial testimony. That use doesn't require an accusation.
questions.e: Under Doyle, post-Miranda silence can't be used to impeach. Pre-arrest and pre-Miranda silence may be used to impeach a defendant who testifies. Adoption by silence requires an accusation that would naturally call for a denial.

questions.tag: Rule 801(d)(1)(A) as amended Dec. 1, 2026
questions.q:
A federal assault trial begins in January 2027. Witness Lucia Ford told a detective in an unsworn, recorded interview that she saw the defendant pull a knife. At trial, Ford testifies that the defendant's hands were empty. The prosecutor confronts her with the interview, and she denies saying it. The prosecutor then plays the recording and asks the court to let the jury use it as proof that the defendant had a knife.

How should the court rule?
o: The recording may be used only to impeach Ford, because her earlier statement wasn't given under penalty of perjury.
The recording is inadmissible hearsay, because Ford didn't adopt it at trial.
The recording may be used as substantive evidence, because Ford testifies, is subject to cross about it, and it is inconsistent with her testimony.
The recording is admissible only as a recorded recollection.
The recording may be used substantively only if Ford is unavailable.
oe: That was the rule until Dec. 1, 2026. The amendment deleted the oath-and-proceeding requirement, and it governs proceedings begun after that date.
Rule 801(d)(1)(A) doesn't require the witness to adopt the statement. Its point is to reach statements the witness now contradicts.

Correct. As amended Dec. 1, 2026, Rule 801(d)(1)(A) requires only that the declarant testify, be subject to cross about the statement, and that the statement be inconsistent with her testimony. An unsworn statement now comes in substantively, with no limiting instruction. Rule 613(b)'s foundation was laid when she was confronted and denied it.
Rule 803(5) requires a witness who lacks memory and vouches for the record. Ford remembers and contradicts it.
Rule 801(d)(1) is built on the declarant testifying. Unavailability belongs to Rule 804.
questions.e: Under Rule 801(d)(1)(A), effective Dec. 1, 2026, a testifying witness's inconsistent statement is substantive evidence even if unsworn. The old rule required a statement under penalty of perjury at a proceeding or deposition. Rule 613(b) still governs extrinsic proof.

questions.tag: Rule 803(5): the witness must vouch
questions.q:
At a November 2026 trial, the prosecution calls Dwayne Hollis, who signed a written statement for police the night of a shooting naming the shooter. On the stand, Hollis says he doesn't remember the events. Asked about the statement, he says: "That's my signature, but I'd been drinking all day. I'd have signed anything, and I can't say it's right." The detective who wrote it down testifies that he recorded Hollis's words accurately.

Is the statement admissible as a recorded recollection?
o: Yes, because it was made when the events were fresh and Hollis now lacks memory.
Yes, because the detective's testimony about accuracy satisfies the foundation.
Yes, and it may be received as an exhibit offered by the prosecution.
No, because Hollis doesn't vouch that the statement accurately reflected his knowledge when he made it.
No, because a recorded recollection must be in the witness's own handwriting.
oe: Freshness and lack of memory are two of the four requirements. The record must also reflect the witness's knowledge accurately, and here no one can vouch for that.
In a two-person record, the recorder can vouch that he transcribed accurately. But the witness must still vouch that what he said was true, and Hollis disowns it.
Even a proper recorded recollection may be read into evidence but received as an exhibit only if offered by an adverse party.

Correct. The Johnson v. State foundation has four parts: firsthand knowledge, made when fresh, insufficient present memory, and the witness's vouching for accuracy. Hollis refuses to vouch, so Rule 803(5) fails.
A record the witness "made or adopted" qualifies. Adopting a statement someone else wrote is enough.
questions.e: A Rule 803(5) recorded recollection requires firsthand knowledge, a record made or adopted when fresh, insufficient present memory, and the witness's vouching for accuracy (Johnson v. State). It is read in, not received as an exhibit unless the adverse party offers it.

questions.tag: Rule 803(3) vs. 803(4): present and past pain
questions.q:
Tina Marr sues for back injuries from a fall in a store. Her coworker would testify to three statements Marr made to her:

I. Two days after the fall: "My back is killing me right now. I can barely sit."
II. A month after the fall: "Last week my back hurt so badly I couldn't sleep."
III. Two days after the fall: "This all started when I slipped on that grease."

The coworker has no medical role. Which statements are admissible to prove Marr's pain or its cause?
o: I only.
I and II only.
I and III only.
II and III only.
I, II, and III.
oe: Correct. Item I describes then-existing pain and is admissible under Rule 803(3) whoever hears it. Item II describes past pain, which Rule 803(3) excludes as memory, and Rule 803(4) doesn't apply because the coworker wasn't consulted for diagnosis or treatment. Item III describes cause, which Rule 803(4) covers only when made for medical purposes.
Item II looks backward. Rule 803(3) covers only a then-existing condition, and statements of memory are excluded.
Item III states past events and cause to a layperson. Rule 803(3) doesn't cover it, and Rule 803(4) requires a medical purpose.
Items II and III both fail, for the reasons above, and Item I qualifies.
Only the statement of present pain qualifies.
questions.e: Rule 803(3) covers then-existing physical condition (pain) said to anyone, but not past pain or its cause. Rule 803(4) reaches past symptoms and general cause only when the statement is made for medical diagnosis or treatment.

questions.tag: Rule 803(6)(C): a one-off memo isn't regular practice
questions.q:
After the first fire in its 30-year history, Tarn Manufacturing's CEO asked the plant manager to "write up what you find out." Over two weeks, the plant manager interviewed workers and wrote a memo concluding that a contractor's welding torch caused the fire. Tarn has never prepared such a memo before. In Tarn's suit against the contractor, Tarn offers the memo through its records custodian.

Is the memo admissible as a business record?
o: Yes, because it was made by an employee with a duty to report, at or near the time of the investigation.
Yes, unless the contractor shows that the memo lacks trustworthiness.
No, because making such a memo wasn't a regular practice of Tarn's business.
Yes, as a public record of a factual investigation.
No, because the plant manager must testify in person.
oe: Timeliness and duty are part of the foundation, but Rule 803(6) also requires that making the record be a regular practice of the activity.
The opponent's burden under Rule 803(6)(E) arises only after Rules 803(6)(A)–(D) are met. Regular practice is missing.

Correct. Rule 803(6)(B)–(C) requires that the record be kept in the course of a regularly conducted activity and that making it be a regular practice. A one-time memo commissioned after a unique event fails. Its preparation as a dispute loomed also raises the Palmer concern now in Rule 803(6)(E).
Tarn is a private company. Rule 803(8) covers public offices.
A custodian or other qualified witness, or a Rule 902(11) certification, can lay the foundation. The flaw is the lack of regular practice.
questions.e: Rule 803(6) requires a record made at or near the time by someone with knowledge, kept in the course of a regularly conducted activity, as a regular practice, shown by a qualified witness or certification. The opponent then may show lack of trustworthiness. One-off and litigation-driven reports fail (Palmer).

questions.tag: Rule 804(b)(3): civil liability, no corroboration needed
questions.q:
A fence company sues Jake Moss for damage done when Moss's car crashed through its fence at 2 a.m. Moss says his friend Rob Tully borrowed the car and was driving. Tully died last month. Moss offers testimony from Tully's brother that a week after the crash Tully told him, privately, "I'm the one who wrecked Jake's car into that fence. Don't tell anyone." The company objects that the statement is uncorroborated hearsay.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because a statement against interest needs corroborating circumstances indicating trustworthiness.
Admit it as a statement against interest, because it exposed Tully to civil liability, and corroboration is required only for criminal-liability statements in criminal cases.
Exclude it, because a statement made in private to a relative isn't against interest.
Admit it, because Tully's death makes all of his statements admissible.
Exclude it, because Moss, as the party who benefits from the statement, can't offer it.
oe: The corroboration requirement in Rule 804(b)(3)(B) applies only to a statement offered in a criminal case as one that tends to expose the declarant to criminal liability.

Correct. Tully is unavailable because he died (Rule 804(a)(4)). A reasonable person wouldn't admit wrecking another's car into a fence unless it were true, because the admission exposes him to civil liability. In a civil case, Rule 804(b)(3) requires no corroboration.
The test is objective, about whether a reasonable person would make the statement only if true. A private admission to family still exposes the speaker to liability.
Unavailability is only a prerequisite. The statement must still fit an exception in Rule 804(b).
Any party may offer a statement against interest. It isn't limited to use against the declarant.
questions.e: Rule 804(b)(3) admits an unavailable declarant's statement that a reasonable person would make only if true because it was so contrary to pecuniary, proprietary, or penal interest, or to civil liability. Corroboration is required only for penal-interest statements in criminal cases.

questions.tag: Rule 803(16): ancient documents after 2017
questions.q:
In a 2026 boundary dispute, Elm Farms offers a 1987 county newspaper article reporting that a stone wall marked "the long-accepted line between the Elm and Birch properties." The article came from the paper's bound archive at the county library. Birch Orchards objects that the article is hearsay.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude it, because newspaper articles are hearsay with no applicable exception.
Admit it only if the reporter is shown to be unavailable.
Admit it only under the residual exception, after written notice.
Exclude it, because the 2017 amendment abolished the ancient-documents exception.
Admit it under the ancient-documents exception, because it was prepared before January 1, 1998, and its authenticity is established.
oe: Rule 803(16) still covers statements in documents prepared before January 1, 1998, whose authenticity is established.
Rule 803(16) is an 803 exception, so availability doesn't matter.
Rule 807 applies only to statements not admissible under Rules 803 or 804. This one is admissible under Rule 803(16).
The 2017 amendment didn't abolish the exception. It limited it to documents prepared before 1998.

Correct. Since 2017, Rule 803(16) covers statements in a document prepared before January 1, 1998, whose authenticity is established. The 1987 article qualifies. A newspaper is self-authenticating under Rule 902(6), and Rule 901(b)(8)'s 20-year test also fits.
questions.e: Rule 803(16) now admits statements in authenticated documents prepared before January 1, 1998. Authentication (Rule 901(b)(8): 20 years old, unsuspicious, found where it would likely be, or Rule 902) is a separate hurdle from hearsay.

questions.tag: Shepard: no settled hopeless expectation; looking backward
questions.q:
In a federal murder prosecution, the government offers testimony from the victim's nurse. Two days after the victim fell ill, she told the nurse, "My husband poisoned my coffee. I'm sure of it." At the time, the victim asked whether she would be well enough for a trip next month, and the doctors had told her she was improving. She relapsed and died three weeks later.

Is the statement admissible?
o: Yes, as a dying declaration, because the victim later died from the poisoning.
Yes, as a statement of the victim's then-existing state of mind.
No, because she didn't believe her death was imminent, and her statement looks backward to another person's act.
Yes, as a statement for medical diagnosis, because it identifies the cause of her illness.
No, because a dying declaration is admissible only in civil cases.
oe: Rule 804(b)(2) looks to the declarant's belief when she spoke. Death that happens later doesn't satisfy it without "a settled hopeless expectation" of imminent death.
Rule 803(3) excludes "a statement of memory or belief to prove the fact remembered or believed." Shepard rejected this route for a backward-looking accusation.

Correct. Shepard v. United States held that the statement wasn't a dying declaration: she planned a trip and was told she was improving, so she lacked a settled hopeless expectation of death. It also wasn't admissible as state of mind, because it looked backward to her husband's act.
Rule 803(4) reaches general cause pertinent to treatment, not the identity of a person at fault.
Rule 804(b)(2) applies in homicide prosecutions and civil cases.
questions.e: A Rule 804(b)(2) dying declaration requires a belief that death is imminent when the statement is made (Shepard). Rule 803(3) excludes memory or belief offered to prove the fact remembered, especially accusations about another person's past acts.

questions.tag: Rule 902(11) certification for a business record
questions.q:
In a federal fraud trial, the government offers a bank's account statements to trace stolen funds. It calls no bank witness. Instead, it gave the defense written notice before trial and made available a certification from the bank's records custodian. The certification attests that the records were made at or near the time by people with knowledge, kept in the regular course of business, and made as a regular practice. The defense objects that no live witness laid a foundation and that the government hasn't shown the records are trustworthy.

How should the court rule?
o: Sustain the objection, because Rule 803(6) requires a custodian or other qualified witness to testify in person.
Sustain the objection, because the proponent must prove that business records are trustworthy.
Overrule the objection, because a Rule 902(11) certification can satisfy the foundation, and the opponent bears the burden of showing untrustworthiness.
Overrule the objection, because bank records are public records under Rule 803(8).
Sustain the objection, because certified records are testimonial and require the custodian's live testimony.
oe: Rule 803(6)(D) allows the foundation to be shown "by a certification that complies with Rule 902(11) or (12)."
Since 2014, Rule 803(6)(E) puts the burden on the opponent to show untrustworthiness.

Correct. With advance written notice and the record made available, a Rule 902(11) certification authenticates a domestic business record and satisfies Rule 803(6)(A)–(D). The opponent must then show lack of trustworthiness under Rule 803(6)(E).
A private bank isn't a public office.
Records kept in the ordinary course of business are generally nontestimonial, unlike lab certificates prepared for trial.
questions.e: Rule 803(6)(D) can be met by a Rule 902(11) or (12) certification, with notice. Under Rule 803(6)(E), the opponent must show untrustworthiness. Ordinary business records are generally nontestimonial.

questions.tag: Bullcoming: a surrogate supervisor
questions.q:
In a federal DUI-manslaughter trial, the prosecution offers a signed laboratory report stating that the defendant's blood-alcohol content was 0.17. The analyst who ran the test is on extended leave. Instead, the lab supervisor testifies. She didn't perform or observe the test, but she reviewed the paperwork and certifies that the lab's procedures were followed. The defense objects under the Confrontation Clause.

How should the court rule?
o: Overrule the objection, because the supervisor is available for cross-examination about the lab's procedures.
Overrule the objection, because lab reports are business records and so are nontestimonial.
Sustain the objection, because the defendant has a right to confront the analyst who made the certification, and a surrogate isn't enough.
Overrule the objection, because the report is offered only as the basis for the supervisor's opinion.
Sustain the objection only if the report was notarized.
oe: In Bullcoming, the Court held that cross-examining a surrogate who didn't perform or observe the test doesn't satisfy the Clause.
A forensic report made to prove a fact at trial is testimonial (Melendez-Diaz). Calling it a business record doesn't change that.

Correct. Under Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming, a forensic report certifying a test result is testimonial. The analyst who certified it must be available for cross unless he is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross. A supervisor who neither ran nor watched the test is a surrogate.
Smith v. Arizona rejected the "not for its truth" basis theory. A report that supports an opinion only if true is offered for its truth.
Bullcoming's report wasn't sworn. Formality is one factor, not a requirement.
questions.e: Forensic certifications made for trial are testimonial (Melendez-Diaz). A surrogate witness who didn't perform or observe the test can't satisfy the Clause (Bullcoming), and basis testimony conveys the analyst's statements for their truth (Smith v. Arizona).

questions.tag: Confrontation in a civil case; Rule 803(8)(A)(iii)
questions.q:
In a civil wrongful-death suit against a nursing home, the plaintiff offers the factual findings of a state health-department investigator. After a formal investigation, the investigator concluded that the home's staff failed to turn the decedent as required. The investigator has since died. The nursing home objects that admitting the findings violates its right to confront witnesses against it, and that the findings are hearsay.

Which ruling is correct?
o: Exclude the findings, because they are testimonial and the home had no chance to cross-examine the investigator.
Exclude the findings, because Rule 803(8) applies only when the official who made the record testifies.
Exclude the findings, because Rule 803(8) bars investigative findings offered against a private party.
Admit the findings only if the plaintiff shows the investigator is unavailable.
Admit the findings under Rule 803(8)(A)(iii), unless the home shows they are untrustworthy. The Confrontation Clause doesn't apply in civil cases.
oe: The Confrontation Clause guarantees rights "to the accused" in criminal prosecutions, not to civil litigants.
Rule 803 exceptions apply regardless of the declarant's availability, and the record itself is the evidence.
Rule 803(8)(A)(iii) admits factual findings in civil cases against any party. Its limit applies only in criminal cases, where findings may be used only against the government.
Unavailability isn't required under Rule 803.

Correct. Rule 803(8)(A)(iii) admits factual findings from a legally authorized investigation in a civil case, and Beech Aircraft extends that to opinions and conclusions. The opponent bears the burden of showing untrustworthiness. The Sixth Amendment protects only the accused.
questions.e: The Confrontation Clause protects only criminal defendants. In civil cases, Rule 803(8)(A)(iii) admits investigative findings, including conclusions (Beech Aircraft), unless the opponent shows untrustworthiness.

questions.tag: Holmes: an arbitrary third-party-guilt rule
questions.q:
In a state murder trial, DNA and fiber evidence point strongly to Calvin Royce. Royce offers a witness who saw another man, Earl Biggs, running from the victim's building with bloody clothes minutes after the killing. He also offers a witness who heard Biggs say he "had to take care of" the victim. The trial court excludes all of it under a state rule that bars third-party-guilt evidence whenever the prosecution's forensic evidence, viewed alone, strongly supports guilt.

How will a reviewing court most likely rule?
o: Affirm, because states may exclude evidence of third-party guilt that raises only a bare suspicion.
Affirm, because strong forensic evidence makes the defense evidence too weak to matter.
Reverse, because judging defense evidence only by the strength of the prosecution's case is arbitrary and denies a meaningful opportunity to present a complete defense.
Reverse, because the Confrontation Clause guarantees the defendant's right to present third-party-guilt evidence.
Affirm, because the Federal Rules don't govern state trials.
oe: Bare-suspicion rules remain valid, but this rule doesn't evaluate the defense evidence at all. It looks only at the prosecution's case.
This is the reasoning Holmes rejected. The strength of one side's evidence doesn't show that the other side's is weak.

Correct. Holmes v. South Carolina struck down this kind of rule as arbitrary. It doesn't serve the legitimate ends of rules that exclude marginal third-party evidence, and it denies "a meaningful opportunity to present a complete defense."
The right comes from due process and compulsory process (Crane; Holmes). The Confrontation Clause protects against the prosecution's witnesses.
That's true but beside the point. The constitutional limit binds state evidence rules.
questions.e: Under Holmes (with the Washington and Rock cases), evidence rules that are arbitrary or disproportionate to their purposes violate the right to present a complete defense. Chambers adds a test for valid rules applied mechanistically to critical, reliable evidence.

questions.tag: Rule 701: a business owner's particularized knowledge
questions.q:
In a suit against a contractor whose construction blocked the entrance to her bakery for five months, owner Mae Lin testifies to her lost profits. She has run the bakery for 12 years, keeps its books herself, and bases her estimate on her own sales records, seasonal patterns, and costs. She isn't designated as an expert, and the contractor objects that lost-profit projections require expert testimony.

How should the court rule?
o: Sustain the objection, because any projection of future or lost profits requires specialized knowledge.
Overrule the objection, because Lin's opinion rests on particularized knowledge gained from running her own business.
Sustain the objection, because lay opinion may not address damages, which is an ultimate issue.
Overrule the objection, but only if Lin's records are admitted under Rule 803(6) first.
Sustain the objection, because a party can't give opinion testimony about her own claim.
oe: The 2000 ACN to Rule 701 recognizes a business owner's lay opinion based on particularized knowledge of the business.

Correct. Under Rule 701 and the 2000 ACN, a business owner may give lay opinion on her business's value or projected profits. Such opinions are based on particularized knowledge of her own business, not on specialized expertise. They are rationally based on perception and helpful.
Rule 704(a) allows opinions on ultimate issues. Damages may be the subject of a lay opinion with a proper foundation.
Lin testifies from her own knowledge. Admitting the records isn't a prerequisite.
Parties may testify and give otherwise-proper lay opinions. Interest goes to credibility.
questions.e: A business owner may give lay opinion under Rule 701 on her own business's value or lost profits, based on particularized knowledge of it, as distinct from specialized expertise under Rule 702.

questions.tag: Rule 702(a): helpfulness and common knowledge
questions.q:
In a trademark case, the plaintiff's sauce is sold as "Brisko." It claims that the defendant's "Crisko" sauce is confusingly similar. The plaintiff calls a linguistics professor, who would testify that, in her opinion, "Brisko" and "Crisko" sound alike to ordinary American listeners. The jurors will hear both names spoken. The defendant moves to exclude her.

What is the most likely ruling?
o: Admit it, because the professor is well qualified in linguistics.
Admit it, because Rule 704(a) allows opinions on ultimate issues such as confusion.
Exclude it, because linguistics isn't a science subject to Daubert.
Exclude it, because the opinion is a legal conclusion that tells the jury what result to reach.
Exclude it, because whether two words sound alike to ordinary listeners is within the jurors' common knowledge, so it won't help them.
oe: Qualification is necessary but not sufficient. The testimony must also help the trier of fact.
Rule 704(a) removes the ultimate-issue objection, but the opinion must still satisfy Rule 702(a)'s helpfulness requirement.
Kumho Tire applies gatekeeping to all expert testimony. The issue here is helpfulness, not whether linguistics is a science.
Saying two words sound alike isn't a statement of law. The problem is that jurors can judge it for themselves.

Correct. Rule 702(a) requires that the specialized knowledge help the trier of fact. The outline's example is whether "Match" and "Macho" sound alike. Jurors who hear the words can decide that themselves, so the testimony doesn't help.
questions.e: Rule 702(a) requires that expert knowledge help the trier of fact. Opinions on matters within jurors' common knowledge, like how two words sound, aren't helpful. Technical matters (slip resistance of wet tile) are.

questions.tag: Rule 1007: the opponent's testimony about content
questions.q:
Rida Corp. sues Talon Inc. for late delivery under a written supply contract. Neither side can find the signed original, and there is no evidence of how it was lost. In his deposition, Talon's president testified: "The contract called for delivery by June 1." Rida offers that deposition testimony at trial to prove the contract's delivery term. Talon objects under the best evidence rule.

How should the court rule?
o: Sustain the objection, unless Rida first proves the original was lost without bad faith on Rida's part.
Overrule the objection, because the content of a writing may be proved by the testimony of the party against whom it is offered.
Sustain the objection, because only a duplicate may substitute for a lost original.
Overrule the objection, but only if Talon's president repeats the testimony at trial.
Sustain the objection, because deposition testimony is hearsay.
oe: Rule 1004(a) is one route, but Rule 1007 is an independent route that doesn't depend on why the original is missing.

Correct. Rule 1007 allows proof of a writing's content by the testimony, deposition, or written statement of the party against whom it is offered, without accounting for the original. Talon's president testifying for Talon qualifies.
Duplicates are one route (Rule 1003). Rules 1004 through 1007 offer others.
Rule 1007 expressly includes "deposition" testimony. No repetition at trial is needed.
Offered against Talon, its president's statement on a matter within the scope of his position is an opposing party's statement (Rule 801(d)(2)(D)).
questions.e: Rule 1002 requires an original to prove content unless an exception applies: duplicates (1003), lost or unobtainable originals (1004), certified public records (1005), summaries (1006), or the opponent's own testimony or written statement (1007).

questions.tag: Rule 502(d): a federal non-waiver order binds state courts
questions.q:
In a federal antitrust case, the court entered an order under Rule 502(d) providing that production of privileged material in discovery "shall not constitute a waiver in this or any other proceeding." Kellan Corp. produced a privileged memo from its general counsel. Later, in a related state-court suit, the plaintiff argues that Kellan waived the privilege by producing the memo in the federal case.

What is the correct result?
o: Waiver, because state law governs privilege in state court.
Waiver, unless Kellan shows the production was inadvertent and it took reasonable steps to prevent and fix it.
No waiver, because a Rule 502(d) order binds the parties but not other courts.
No waiver, because a federal court's Rule 502(d) order that disclosure isn't a waiver binds all other federal and state proceedings.
Waiver of the memo and of all communications on the same subject.
oe: Rule 502(f) makes the rule apply in state proceedings, and Rule 502(d) orders bind state courts.
Rule 502(b)'s inadvertence test applies when no order governs. A Rule 502(d) order replaces it.
That describes a party agreement under Rule 502(e). A court order binds everyone.

Correct. Under Rule 502(d), a federal court may order that a disclosure connected with its litigation isn't a waiver. The order binds "any other Federal or State proceeding," and Rule 502(f) confirms the rule applies in state proceedings.
Subject-matter waiver under Rule 502(a) requires an intentional waiver. The order means there is none.
questions.e: Rule 502(d) orders bind all federal and state proceedings. Rule 502(b) protects inadvertent disclosures with reasonable precautions and prompt rectification. Rule 502(a) limits subject-matter waiver to intentional disclosures, where fairness requires it. Rule 502(e) agreements bind only the parties.

questions.tag: Tanner: nonjuror evidence of misconduct
questions.q:
After Vera Holt's conviction for securities fraud, she moves for a new trial. She supports the motion with two affidavits. The first, from a juror, says four jurors drank pitchers of beer at lunch every day of trial and dozed through afternoon testimony. The second, from a waiter at the café across from the courthouse, says he served those jurors two pitchers of beer at lunch each day.

Which affidavit may the court consider?
o: Both, because intoxication during trial is an outside influence on the jury.
Neither, because Rule 606(b) bars any evidence of juror misconduct once a verdict is returned.
Only the waiter's affidavit, because Rule 606(b) limits jurors' testimony, not evidence from people who aren't jurors.
Only the juror's affidavit, because a juror is the best witness to what happened among jurors.
Both, because the Sixth Amendment right to a competent jury overrides Rule 606(b).
oe: Tanner held that drugs and alcohol are "no more an 'outside influence' than a virus, poorly prepared food, or a lack of sleep."
Rule 606(b) restricts a juror's own testimony and affidavits. It doesn't bar evidence from others.

Correct. Under Tanner, juror testimony about juror intoxication is barred, because intoxication isn't an outside influence. Tanner relied on other safeguards: observation during trial, juror reports before the verdict, and nonjuror evidence of misconduct after it. The waiter's affidavit is that kind of evidence.
The juror's affidavit is exactly what Rule 606(b) and Tanner exclude.
Tanner held that Rule 606(b)'s bar doesn't violate the Sixth Amendment in this setting.
questions.e: Rule 606(b) bars jurors from testifying about internal matters such as intoxication (Tanner). Misconduct may still be proved by nonjuror evidence, and by juror reports made before the verdict.

questions.tag: Rules 601–603: a young child's competency
questions.q:
In a federal prosecution for abusive sexual contact, the government calls the five-year-old victim. At a competency hearing, she says that telling a lie is "saying something that didn't happen" and that lying is bad. She promises to tell the truth and describes the events, though her account of the time of day and the room's furniture varies from an earlier interview. The defense argues she is too young and too inconsistent to testify.

How should the court rule?
o: She may not testify, because children under seven are presumed incompetent.
She may not testify unless the court finds by a preponderance that her account is accurate.
She may not testify unless a psychologist certifies her ability to tell fantasy from reality.
She may testify, but only through a recorded interview, not live.
She may testify, because every person is presumed competent, and inconsistencies go to the weight of her testimony.
oe: The age-based common-law presumptions are gone. Rule 601 makes every person competent unless a rule provides otherwise, and a federal statute presumes children competent.
The judge doesn't decide whether testimony is accurate. Personal knowledge needs only evidence sufficient to support a finding (Rule 602), and credibility is for the jury.
No expert certification is required. The court asks about the ability to perceive, remember, communicate, and understand the duty to tell the truth.
A competent child testifies live, subject to cross.

Correct. Rule 601 presumes competence, and the child shows she understands the duty to tell the truth. She can affirm it in a form suited to her age (Rule 603), and she perceived the events (Rule 602). Inconsistent details are for cross-examination and the jury.
questions.e: Rule 601 presumes every witness competent, and federal law presumes children competent. Rule 602 requires personal knowledge sufficient to support a finding, and Rule 603 an oath or affirmation. Inconsistencies go to credibility.

questions.tag: Rule 401(b): materiality from the substantive law
questions.q:
Joe Rinaldi, a bar owner, is charged under a statute making it a crime to sell alcohol to anyone under 21. The statute imposes strict liability, and the defendant's belief about the buyer's age isn't an element or a defense. Rinaldi offers the 19-year-old buyer's fake driver's license, showing her age as 23, to prove he reasonably believed she was of age.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit it, because it has a tendency to make Rinaldi's reasonable belief more probable.
Admit it with a limiting instruction that it bears only on Rinaldi's state of mind.
Exclude it under Rule 403 only, because it might confuse the jury.
Exclude it as irrelevant, because Rinaldi's belief isn't a fact of consequence under a strict-liability statute.
Admit it, because a defendant always has a constitutional right to present evidence of good faith.
oe: Probativeness is half of Rule 401. The fact must also be "of consequence in determining the action" (materiality).
An instruction can't make immaterial evidence relevant.
The evidence fails the threshold of Rule 401, before any Rule 403 balancing.

Correct. Rule 401(b) requires that the fact be of consequence, and the substantive law defines what is. Under a strict-liability statute, Rinaldi's belief about age is immaterial (compare Wingate and the Egelhoff voluntary-intoxication statute), so the license is irrelevant under Rule 402.
The right to present a defense doesn't require admitting evidence on an issue the substantive law makes irrelevant (the Egelhoff case).
questions.e: Under Rule 401, relevance requires both probativeness and materiality, and the substantive law decides which facts are of consequence. A statute can make a probative fact immaterial.

questions.tag: Old Chief doesn't reach a 404(b) purpose
questions.q:
Rex Hale is charged in one indictment with (1) possessing cocaine with intent to distribute and (2) being a felon in possession of a firearm. His prior felony is a 2019 conviction for cocaine distribution. Hale offers to stipulate that he is a convicted felon. His defense on count 1 is that he was only a visitor in the apartment and didn't know the drugs were there. The government wants to prove the nature of the 2019 conviction to show knowledge and intent on count 1.

Which ruling is correct?
o: The court must accept the stipulation on count 2 but may admit the 2019 conviction on count 1 to show knowledge and intent, if it passes Rule 403, with a limiting instruction.
Under Old Chief, the government may never mention the nature of the 2019 conviction once Hale offers to stipulate.
The court may reject the stipulation and let the government prove the nature of the conviction on count 2, because the prosecution may prove its case its own way.
The 2019 conviction is inadmissible on count 1, because a prior drug crime can show only propensity.
The 2019 conviction is admissible on both counts without any instruction, because Hale put his knowledge in issue.
oe: Correct. Old Chief requires the court to accept a stipulation to legal status on the felon-in-possession count. But its holding is confined to status elements. On count 1, a prior distribution conviction may be offered under Rule 404(b)(2) to show knowledge and intent, which Hale disputes. It must pass the Huddleston steps and Rule 403, and Rule 105 entitles him to an instruction on request.
Old Chief addresses proof of status. It doesn't bar the same evidence offered for a separate, proper purpose on another count.
For a status element, Old Chief holds that refusing the stipulation and proving the name of the offense is an abuse of discretion.
Knowledge and intent are proper Rule 404(b)(2) purposes when the defendant claims he didn't know about the drugs.
On count 2, the stipulation controls. On count 1, Hale is entitled to a limiting instruction on request.
questions.e: Old Chief requires accepting a stipulation to a prior-felony status element. It doesn't bar the prior offered for a Rule 404(b)(2) purpose on a disputed issue, which remains subject to Rule 403 and a Rule 105 instruction.

questions.tag: Rule 408: no dispute, no protection
questions.q:
Garnet Supply delivered $50,000 of lumber to Lomax Builders. Before any lawsuit, Lomax's owner emailed Garnet: "I know we owe the full $50,000 and the lumber was fine, but cash is tight. Will you take $30,000 to close this out?" Garnet refused and sued. At trial, Lomax claims for the first time that the lumber was defective. Garnet offers the email.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because Rule 408 bars any offer to accept less than the amount claimed.
Admit it, because Rule 408 applies only to a claim disputed as to validity or amount when the statement is made.
Admit it only to impeach Lomax's owner if he testifies that the lumber was defective.
Exclude it, because statements made before a lawsuit is filed are protected.
Admit it only to show bias.
oe: Rule 408 protects compromise of a disputed claim, not a request to pay less on an admitted debt.

Correct. Rule 408(a) applies to compromise of "a claim that was disputed" as to validity or amount. Lomax conceded both the debt and the quality, so there was nothing to compromise. A plea to pay less on an undisputed debt isn't protected, and the email comes in as Lomax's own statement.
Because Rule 408 doesn't apply, the email is admissible substantively. And even where Rule 408 applies, it bars impeachment by inconsistency.
Rule 408 can protect negotiations before suit if there is a dispute. Here there was none.
Bias is a Rule 408(b) permitted purpose for evidence the rule otherwise covers. This email isn't covered.
questions.e: Rule 408 requires a claim disputed as to validity or amount when the offer or statement is made. Asking for a discount on an admitted debt isn't a compromise and gets no protection.

questions.tag: Mezzanatto: waiving Rule 410 for impeachment
questions.q:
To get a proffer session with federal prosecutors, Tony Vega signed an agreement stating that if he testified at trial inconsistently with his proffer statements, those statements could be used to impeach him. In the session, Vega admitted being at the warehouse during a drug sale. No plea agreement resulted. At trial, Vega testifies that he was never at the warehouse, and the prosecutor offers his proffer statement on cross.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because Rule 410's protections can't be waived.
Admit it, because Rule 410 permits statements from plea discussions to be used for impeachment in any event.
Admit it to impeach, because a defendant may knowingly and voluntarily waive Rule 410, and Vega did.
Exclude it, because plea statements may be used only in a later perjury prosecution.
Exclude it, because statements to prosecutors are protected only if a guilty plea results.
oe: Mezzanatto held that Rule 410's protections are waivable, like many constitutional rights.
Congress removed the impeachment use from Rule 410 in 1975. Absent a waiver, the statement would be barred.

Correct. United States v. Mezzanatto upheld a knowing and voluntary agreement allowing plea-discussion statements to impeach a defendant who testifies inconsistently. The statements otherwise fall within Rule 410(a)(4).
Rule 410(b)(2) is one exception (perjury, made under oath, on the record, with counsel), but a valid waiver is another route.
Rule 410(a)(4) protects discussions that didn't result in a guilty plea, which is the situation here.
questions.e: Under Rule 410(a)(4), statements in plea discussions with a prosecutor that don't produce a guilty plea are inadmissible against the defendant, even to impeach. Under Mezzanatto, a defendant may knowingly and voluntarily waive that protection.

questions.tag: Rule 407: firing an employee as a remedial measure
questions.q:
A Fleet Movers van ran a stop sign and struck cyclist Abby Chen. The next day, Fleet fired the driver. Chen sues Fleet, alleging that the driver was negligent and that Fleet is vicariously liable. Fleet admits that the driver was its employee acting within the scope of employment. Chen offers evidence of the firing to show that the driver was at fault.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit it, because Rule 407 covers only physical repairs and design changes.
Admit it, because firing the driver is an admission by conduct.
Admit it to show Fleet's control over the driver.
Admit it, because it is offered to prove the driver's negligence, not Fleet's.
Exclude it, because firing the driver is a measure that would have made the accident less likely, offered to prove culpable conduct.
oe: Rule 407 covers any "measures" that would have made the injury less likely. Disciplining or firing a negligent employee qualifies.
That is precisely the inference Rule 407 forbids: that a post-accident measure shows fault.
Control is a permitted purpose only "if disputed." Fleet concedes employment and scope.
Chen's claim against Fleet depends on the driver's negligence. Offering the firing to prove it is offering it to prove negligence or culpable conduct.
Correct. Removing an unsafe driver is a measure that would have made the collision less likely. Rule 407 bars it to prove negligence or culpable conduct, and no permitted purpose is in dispute.
questions.e: Rule 407 covers any post-injury measure that would have made the harm less likely, including discipline or firing. The "if disputed" purposes (ownership, control, feasibility) apply only when the opponent actually disputes them.

questions.tag: Rule 404(b)(2): motive from discovered embezzlement
questions.q:
Lorna Pace, a bookkeeper, is charged with murdering her employer, Hugh Brandt, who was found dead in his office. The prosecution offers evidence that Pace had embezzled $80,000 from Brandt over two years. It also offers Brandt's email to his lawyer, sent a week before his death, saying he had discovered the theft and would call the police on Monday. Pace has never been charged with embezzlement. She objects that the evidence shows only that she is a thief.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because uncharged crimes are inadmissible under Rule 404(b) without a conviction.
Exclude it, because the desire to avoid punishment is just another form of criminal propensity.
Admit it, because the embezzlement and its discovery give Pace a motive to kill Brandt, a non-propensity purpose, subject to Rule 403 and a limiting instruction.
Admit it only if Pace testifies and denies a motive.
Admit it, because Rule 404(b) doesn't apply to acts involving the same victim.
oe: Huddleston requires only evidence from which a jury could reasonably find the act occurred, not a conviction.

Under Kirsch, a motive that is just a desire to commit this kind of crime is propensity. A motive to silence someone who discovered a crime runs through a specific reason to act, not through character.

Correct. The chain goes from embezzlement, to Brandt's discovery and threat to call police, to a reason to stop him, to the killing. No step relies on Pace's character, so motive is a Rule 404(b)(2) purpose. The Huddleston steps follow: 104(b) sufficiency, Rule 403, and a Rule 105 instruction on request.
Motive is part of the prosecution's case-in-chief. It doesn't depend on Pace's testimony.
Rule 404(b) applies to "any other crime, wrong, or act," whoever the victim.
questions.e: Evidence of another act comes in under Rule 404(b)(2) when it proves motive through a non-character chain, such as a reason to silence the person who discovered a crime. It is then subject to Huddleston, Rule 403, and a limiting instruction.

questions.tag: Other acts to prove an employer's notice
questions.q:
A delivery driver for Route One Logistics rammed Grace Toll's car in a road-rage incident. Toll sues Route One for negligent retention, alleging that it kept the driver on despite knowing he was dangerous. She offers three customer complaints, received by Route One's safety manager during the prior year, each describing the driver tailgating and threatening other motorists.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude them, because Rule 404(b) bars other acts offered to show the driver's propensity for road rage.
Exclude them, because character may be proved only by reputation or opinion.
Admit them, but only if the driver testifies.
Admit them, because they show Route One knew of the risk, which is an element of negligent retention and not a propensity use.
Exclude them as hearsay, because they are customers' out-of-court statements.
oe: The complaints aren't offered to show the driver acted in character on the day of the crash. They show what Route One knew.
In negligent retention, the employee's dangerousness is an essential element, so Rule 405(b) allows specific instances. And the employer's notice isn't a character use at all.
Admissibility doesn't depend on the driver's testimony.

Correct. Negligent retention requires proof that the employer knew or should have known the employee was dangerous. Complaints received by the employer prove notice, a non-character purpose. To the extent the driver's dangerousness is an element, Rule 405(b) permits specific instances. Rule 403 still applies.
Offered to show that Route One received complaints, the statements aren't offered for their truth. That is notice, a non-hearsay use.
questions.e: Other acts offered to show what a party knew (notice) are a non-character use. When character is an essential element, as in negligent retention or entrustment, Rule 405(b) permits specific instances.

questions.tag: Rule 413: the 15-day disclosure requirement
questions.q:
Neil Crane is charged with aggravated sexual abuse. Six days before trial, the prosecution first disclosed a witness who would testify that Crane tried to force himself on her four years ago, before she broke free. The prosecution offers no explanation for the timing, and Crane objects that he has no time to investigate.

What is the best ruling?
o: Admit it, because Rule 413 evidence is admissible regardless of notice.
Admit it, because Rule 404(b)(3) requires only reasonable notice, and six days is reasonable.
Exclude it, because an attempted assault isn't a "sexual assault" under Rule 413.
Exclude it, because Rule 413 applies only to prior convictions.
Don't admit it as offered: Rule 413(b) requires disclosure at least 15 days before trial unless the court allows a later time for good cause, and none has been shown.
oe: Rule 413(b) imposes a specific disclosure requirement.
Rule 413(b) sets its own 15-day minimum for propensity evidence offered under that rule.
Rule 413(d) defines sexual assault to include an attempt.
No conviction is required, and the Huddleston standard applies.

Correct. The attempt qualifies under Rule 413(d)'s definition. But Rule 413(b) requires disclosure, including witnesses' statements, at least 15 days before trial "or at a later time that the court allows for good cause." With no good cause shown, the court shouldn't admit it as offered (it may consider a continuance).
questions.e: Rules 413–415 require disclosure at least 15 days before trial or at a later time the court allows for good cause. Their definitions include attempts. Once admitted, the evidence may be used for propensity, subject to Rule 403.

questions.tag: Rule 609(a)(1): punishable by exactly one year
questions.q:
In a civil trial, the defendant seeks to impeach the plaintiff's witness with her conviction, three years ago, for misdemeanor shoplifting. The offense is punishable by up to one year in jail, and she was sentenced to 30 days. The offense's elements require taking property with intent to deprive the owner, but not any false statement.

Is the conviction admissible to impeach her?
o: Yes, because theft is inherently a crime of dishonesty.
Yes, subject to Rule 403, because she was sentenced to jail time.
Yes, because any conviction less than 10 years old may be used.
No, because it isn't punishable by more than one year and its elements don't require a dishonest act or false statement.
Yes, but only by asking about the underlying act under Rule 608(b), not by proving the conviction.
oe: The ACN (2006) limits Rule 609(a)(2) to crimes whose elements require proof of a dishonest act or false statement, such as fraud or perjury. Theft generally doesn't qualify.
Rule 609(a)(1) looks to the maximum punishment, which must exceed one year. The sentence imposed doesn't matter.
Recency matters only once a conviction qualifies under Rule 609(a).

Correct. A crime punishable by exactly one year isn't "punishable by ... imprisonment for more than one year" under Rule 609(a)(1). Shoplifting's elements don't require a dishonest act or false statement, so Rule 609(a)(2) doesn't apply either.
Rule 608(b) allows inquiry only into acts probative of truthfulness. Courts generally don't treat simple theft as such an act, and the conviction itself is governed by Rule 609.
questions.e: Rule 609(a)(1) requires a crime punishable by death or imprisonment for more than one year. Rule 609(a)(2) requires elements involving a dishonest act or false statement. Theft and shoplifting ordinarily satisfy neither.

questions.tag: Rule 609(c): pardon followed by a later felony
questions.q:
In a federal drug trial, the defense wants to impeach the government's informant with his 2018 felony conviction for burglary. In 2021 the governor pardoned him after a finding that he had been rehabilitated. In 2023 he was convicted of felony assault, punishable by up to five years. The government argues that the pardon bars use of the 2018 conviction.

Is the pardon a bar?
o: Yes, because any pardon bars use of the pardoned conviction.
No, because a rehabilitation pardon bars use only if the person hasn't been convicted of a later crime punishable by more than one year.
Yes, unless the 2018 conviction involved dishonesty.
No, because only a pardon based on innocence bars impeachment.
Yes, because a pardoned conviction is treated as if it never occurred.
oe: Rule 609(c) bars use only if its conditions are met.

Correct. Under Rule 609(c)(1), a pardon based on a finding of rehabilitation bars use only if the person hasn't been convicted of a later crime punishable by more than one year. The 2023 felony lifts the bar, so the 2018 conviction may be used if it passes Rule 609(a)(1)(A)'s Rule 403 test.
Rule 609(c) turns on the basis of the pardon and later convictions, not on whether the crime was crimen falsi.
Rule 609(c)(2) also bars use after a pardon based on innocence, but a rehabilitation pardon can bar use too under Rule 609(c)(1).
Rule 609(c) has its own conditions. It doesn't erase the conviction for all purposes.
questions.e: Under Rule 609(c), a pardon or annulment based on innocence bars use. One based on rehabilitation bars use only if no later conviction for a crime punishable by more than one year follows.

questions.tag: Rule 610: religion and bias
questions.q:
A patient's estate sues St. Brendan's Hospital, which is owned and operated by a church, for wrongful death. On cross-examination of a defense nurse, the plaintiff's counsel asks two questions: (1) "You're a member of the church that runs St. Brendan's, aren't you?" and (2) "And your faith teaches that lying is a grave sin, so you'd never shade the truth for anyone, would you?"

Which questions are proper?
o: Neither, because Rule 610 bars any reference to a witness's religion.
Both, because a witness's religious beliefs bear on truthfulness.
(1) only, because church membership may be shown to prove bias toward a party, though beliefs may not be used to attack credibility.
(2) only, because it concerns truthfulness rather than affiliation.
(1) only, and only if the nurse first testifies about her religion on direct.
oe: The ACN to Rule 610 says inquiry to show interest or bias because of religious affiliation, as with a church that is a party, isn't within the prohibition.
Rule 610 bars religious beliefs or opinions offered to attack or support credibility.

Correct. Rule 610 bars evidence of religious beliefs to show that a witness's credibility is impaired or enhanced. Question (2) does that. Membership in the church that operates the defendant hospital shows potential bias toward a party, which the ACN permits. That makes (1) proper.
Question (2) uses the nurse's religious beliefs to assess her truthfulness, which is exactly what Rule 610 forbids.
Bias may be explored on cross whether or not the witness raised her religion on direct.
questions.e: Rule 610 bars evidence of a witness's religious beliefs to attack or support credibility. Religious affiliation offered to show bias or interest, as with a church that is a party, isn't barred.

questions.tag: Rule 412(b)(1)(A) and Rule 412(c) procedure
questions.q:
Ty Morrow is charged with sexual abuse. He claims he never had sexual contact with the complainant. The prosecution will offer a nurse's testimony that the complainant had genital injuries consistent with forced intercourse that night. Five days before trial, Morrow moves to admit evidence that the complainant had intercourse with another man that same afternoon, to show another source of the injuries. He explains that he learned of it only the day before.

What is the correct ruling?
o: Deny the motion, because Rule 412 bars all evidence of a victim's sexual behavior in criminal cases.
The court may admit it under the exception for another source of physical evidence, if it allows the late motion for good cause and holds a sealed hearing.
Admit it under the exception for sexual behavior with the accused.
Deny the motion, because a Rule 412 motion filed less than 14 days before trial must be denied.
Admit it as evidence of the victim's character under Rule 404(a)(2)(B).
oe: Rule 412(b)(1) lists exceptions in criminal cases. One fits here.

Correct. Rule 412(b)(1)(A) admits specific instances offered to prove that someone other than the defendant was the source of injury. Rule 412(c) requires a motion at least 14 days before trial unless the court, for good cause, sets a different time. It also requires notice to the victim and an in camera hearing.
Rule 412(b)(1)(B) covers behavior with the accused, offered to prove consent. Morrow denies any contact.
Rule 412(c)(1)(B) allows a later time "for good cause." Learning the facts the day before is a reason to find it.
Rule 404(a)(2)(B) is expressly "subject to the limitations in Rule 412," and sexual behavior isn't a pertinent character trait.
questions.e: In criminal cases, Rule 412(b)(1) admits a victim's sexual behavior only (A) to show another source of semen, injury, or physical evidence, (B) with the accused, or (C) when the Constitution requires. Rule 412(c) requires a motion 14 days before trial (or later for good cause), notice, and a sealed hearing.

questions.tag: Wright v. Doe d. Tatham under the Federal Rules
questions.q:
In a will contest, Arthur Blaine's relatives claim he lacked capacity when he signed his will. The will's proponent offers a dozen letters that Blaine's longtime business associates wrote to him during the year before the will. In them, the associates asked his advice on complex investment and tax matters. The proponent offers the letters to show that people who dealt with him regularly treated him as fully competent.
